money_at_stake.rationale: Three separately-announced, separately-funded programs sit inside this occurrence's window and are additive rather than alternative: the Russian state NSR development plan (about 1.8 to 2 trillion rubles, roughly USD 30bn, across 150+ measures to 2035, of which about 600bn rubles is federal budget), the Canadian Coast Guard icebreaker program (USD 8bn fixed price, Davie), and the US polar icebreaker program (about USD 6.8bn awarded). That is comfortably tens of billions of committed capital and not a hundred, so the band is B10_100. Deliberately NOT a point estimate: the three programs are stated in different currencies over different horizons with different budget-versus-private splits, and adding them into one headline number would create a precision none of the three sources supports.

evidence.claim: Russia's approved Northern Sea Route development plan to 2035 totals almost 1.8 trillion rubles across more than 150 measures, reported as about USD 29.7bn to 30bn, with roughly a third from the federal budget and cargo targets of 150Mt by 2030 and over 200Mt by 2035.
evidence.source_name: TASS, Russian government allocation for Northern Sea Route development by 2035

evidence.claim: Davie secured a USD 8bn fixed-price contract to build six icebreakers for the Canadian Coast Guard, one of the largest recent Arctic shipbuilding programs.
evidence.source_name: gCaptain, Davie adds six Canadian icebreakers to growing Arctic shipbuilding portfolio

evidence.claim: The US Arctic icebreaker expansion has awarded close to USD 6.8bn in shipbuilding contracts, split across Davie Defense (five ships), Rauma (two) and Bollinger (up to four).
evidence.source_name: Marine Insight, Trump's 6.8 billion Arctic icebreaker plan faces scrutiny over no-bid shipbuilding contracts

public_reach.rationale: This is the finding. On the Russian side, which carries most of the money and all of the NSR traffic growth in the signal's thesis, the beneficiaries are Rosatom (state, unlisted), Sovcomflot (sanctioned) and Zvezda (state-controlled): a Western brokerage account cannot reach any of them. On the Western side, the two largest awards go to private yards, Davie (Chantier Davie / Inocea) and Bollinger, with Rauma also private. The listed names that do touch this chain are the Korean yards, and their exposure to THIS occurrence has so far been a liability rather than a revenue line: Samsung Heavy terminated its Arc7 hull cooperation after delivering five of a contracted set, and Hanwha Ocean is carrying six undelivered icebreaking LNG carriers it cannot hand over. A listed issuer whose Arctic exposure is a write-down is not public reach, it is the opposite. Not scored lower than 25 because a real, if second-order, listed set exists (Korean yards on any non-Russian order, marine underwriters, Arctic-adjacent port and equipment names), and establishing whether it is investable is exactly what a chain build is for.

evidence.claim: Samsung Heavy Industries terminated its contract to build icebreaking LNG carrier hulls with Russia's Zvezda shipyard after Western sanctions put the cooperation on hold; the 2020 and 2021 follow-on contracts for 10 more icebreaking LNGCs and seven ice-class shuttle tankers were valued at about USD 3.5bn.
evidence.source_name: gCaptain, Samsung cancels order for icebreaking gas carriers for Russia's sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project

evidence.claim: Hanwha Ocean is carrying hundreds of millions of dollars of financial burden from six icebreaking LNG carriers built for Arctic LNG 2 that remain undelivered under sanctions, with no option beyond waiting for new buyers or selling at a steep discount.
evidence.source_name: The Korea Times, Hanwha Ocean faces mounting costs from blocked icebreaker delivery to Russia

evidence.claim: The US and Canadian icebreaker awards name Davie Defense, Rauma and Bollinger as the building yards; none of the three is a listed issuer.
evidence.source_name: Marine Insight, Trump's 6.8 billion Arctic icebreaker plan faces scrutiny over no-bid shipbuilding contracts

capture_odds.rationale: Genuinely two-sided, so it sits at the middle anchor rather than being rounded toward the story. For capture: polar-class and Arc7 construction is a narrow qualification-gated capability held by a handful of yards worldwide, which is the structural shape that normally holds price. Against capture: the buyers here are sovereign, and sovereign icebreaker procurement is being run no-bid and fixed-price, which caps upside at the contracted number while leaving the yard carrying cost overruns. The Hanwha and Samsung outcomes are the empirical test already run on this exact chain, and the money did not stay with the builder. Scored on that evidence rather than on the concentration argument alone.

evidence.claim: The US icebreaker contracts, close to USD 6.8bn, were awarded without competitive bidding and are under scrutiny for it; the Canadian award is fixed price.
evidence.source_name: Marine Insight, Trump's 6.8 billion Arctic icebreaker plan faces scrutiny over no-bid shipbuilding contracts

evidence.claim: Hanwha Ocean's completed Arc7 carriers are stranded with no viable buyer, so a delivered qualification-gated vessel did not convert into revenue for the yard that built it.
evidence.source_name: The Korea Times, Hanwha Ocean faces mounting costs from blocked icebreaker delivery to Russia

timing_fit.rationale: The money is committed and dated inside the horizon rather than projected into it. The Canadian and US awards are signed contracts with vessels under construction now, and the Russian plan carries an intermediate 2030 cargo milestone well inside the signal's 3 to 5 year window, with the year-round navigation pledge targeting the 2026-2027 season. Not scored higher than 80 because the largest single pool (the Russian plan) runs to 2035, so a meaningful share of it lands past the window this repo underwrites.

evidence.claim: The Russian NSR plan sets cargo traffic targets of 150Mt by 2030 and over 200Mt by 2035, with the build program covering more than 50 icebreakers and ice-class vessels plus ports, terminals and satellites.
evidence.source_name: TASS, Russian government allocation for Northern Sea Route development by 2035

evidence.claim: The Canadian six-icebreaker award is a signed fixed-price contract rather than a proposal, placing the spend inside the current build cycle.
evidence.source_name: gCaptain, Davie adds six Canadian icebreakers to growing Arctic shipbuilding portfolio

notes.text: LEAKY is not a recommendation to drop this signal. The chain build is what would establish whether the second-order listed set (Korean yards on non-Russian orders, polar marine underwriters, Arctic port and equipment names) is real. What this appraisal says is that the headline money, the NSR traffic growth in the card's own thesis, is not the reachable part, so a chain build here should start from the Western icebreaker programs and the insurance link rather than from NSR volumes.
